title: Exaggerating Motion | Why Do Game Characters Move More Dramatically Than Real People?
titleKo: 동작의 과장 | 게임 캐릭터는 왜 현실보다 과장되게 움직일까?
translationScope: Complete current Korean narration with matching five scenes and fourteen paragraphs. No new source facts or game names added.

scenes.title: Why Movements Are Exaggerated
lines: If you freeze a powerful attack in a fighting game, you may see a dramatically twisted waist or an arm stretched unusually far. The movement felt powerful in motion, yet the body can look strange in a single frame. If we restore those poses to a more normal shape, will the attack improve too? Today, we will examine how movement reads on screen, the limits of a character’s skeleton, and, finally, moving slightly past a target and back.

A pose may be deliberately designed to convey power. If we change it based only on its frozen appearance, we can change the impression of the movement. During a broad swing of the arm, the torso must turn with it for the hand to look forceful. With the torso held still, even an arm movement in the same direction can feel weak.

Let's look at Ralf in The King of Fighters XV. When the character on the left punches, watch whether only his hand moves or his chest also turns. A short jab and a broad swing begin with different preparation poses. He draws his arm back, then drives it with his torso. After the attack, he returns to a fighting stance. It is more than the distance his fist travels. The whole body opening and gathering again conveys the force.

scenes.title: More Than the Character Gets Smaller
lines: That difference matters more when the character looks small. Up close, even a slight shoulder movement can communicate a sense of preparation. But when the camera moves farther away, that difference shrinks to a few tiny dots. A movement that looked sufficient while making it can look, in the actual gameplay view, as though the character barely moved.

Now look at Sol in Guilty Gear -Strive-. He wears red and carries a large sword. When he swings the sword sideways, his arm and blade extend far beyond his body. In a rising attack, his silhouette stretches vertically. Even during rapid combat, you can read the direction of the attack. After observing these broad shape changes in gameplay, we will vary only movement amplitude in our comparison.

First, we will compare the same movement in a large view and a small view. Now, we will fix the small view’s camera and playback timing and increase only the shoulder and waist movement. This is exaggeration of movement. It brings out the differences that make an attack readable so that the screen size does not hide them.

For a small character’s attack, first consider whether insufficient movement is draining its power, rather than excessive exaggeration. Even if a movement initially seems sufficient, push it one step further and compare. Keep the movement and camera the same and view it at the actual gameplay size. It becomes easier to judge how well its power comes across.

scenes.title: What the Rig Allows
lines: Even if you want to make the movement larger, the character’s controls may not allow it. Inside a character are reference points linked like bones. Moving them changes the surface of the body. Together, this skeleton and its controls are called a rig.

Think about raising an arm. In a real person, more than the arm rotates: the shoulder’s position and the torso also change. Changing direction around the point where a joint attaches is rotation; moving that point itself is translation. If a rig lets you change only the arm’s angle, while the shoulder’s attachment to the torso stays fixed, creating the pose you want can be difficult.

On screen, we compare a rig with fixed shoulder positions with one whose shoulders can move forward and backward. Even with the same target for the hand, the shape of the shoulder and chest changes. Controls and tools that also handle shoulder translation expand the range of movements you can express. Identify which parts must rotate or move for the intended action, and use the appropriate controls.

scenes.title: The Motion Matters Beyond a Single Pose
lines: Even with more freedom to move the body, making each intermediate pose look attractive is not enough. As the feet push against the ground and the pelvis turns, with the shoulders and arms following, different directions of motion can briefly overlap. The waist and legs may look mismatched in that instant, but in motion, that pose may help create a powerful turn.

So first, watch the entire movement at its actual speed. Check where the force appears to travel, then pause at the moments you need to inspect. If you remove every twist based only on paused poses, you can also lose the flow of the attack. Fix problems with the joints or surface, while preserving the role that each pose plays within the movement.

When Ralf prepares his powerful punch, that connection becomes even clearer. He lowers his body and draws his arm high and back. Then he turns forward and drives his fist out. The preparation and recovery missed in a single impact pose happen before and after it. So, when analyzing an attack, follow the preparation, the strike and the return as one continuous movement. Deciding which moment to exaggerate also depends on that flow.

scenes.title: Passing the Target and Returning
lines: How a pose is reached also affects the sense of power. Moving an object forward and stopping exactly on target looks neat. Moving a little farther and then settling into place can feel like the object is absorbing its momentum. This movement slightly beyond the target is called overshoot.

In our example, the starting point on the floor is zero centimeters, and we mark the target one hundred centimeters ahead. We compare stopping directly at one hundred centimeters with moving to one hundred ten centimeters and returning to one hundred, over the same duration. The second goes ten centimeters past the target and returns. We chose these distances for this comparison; you can adjust them to suit the movement.

The same idea applies not only to position, but also to body size or the shape of extending spikes. Let the spikes reach their largest spread, then shrink a little as they settle. Even a brief change from the largest image to a slightly smaller one in the very next frame can preserve the forceful impression of popping outward.

Exaggerating motion helps communicate the intended action clearly at the actual screen size and playback speed. Choose what moves more and when it overshoots and returns, and even a small character can look powerful.
